96 Plus, retirees’ investments, the affordability agenda and the downsides of a boring job market   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Greg Ip   The Inflation Fight May Be About to Turn Painful   Plus, retirees’ investments, the affordability agenda and the downsides of a boring job market   We may look back on October’s consumer-price index as an inflection point, when the balance of risks flipped toward a painful rather than painless inflation cure.

   The consumer-price index rose 0.4%, and the core index, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3%. Anything over 0.2% is incompatible with the Federal Reserve’s 2% target, and this was the third 0.3% increase in a row.

   Prior hot readings could be chalked up to something specific—energy, or used cars, or cellphone plans. Not this one.  

   You can see this in two Cleveland Fed measures that remove outliers. The median CPI, which tracks the component whose expenditure weight is in the 50th percentile of price changes, rose at a 3.7% annual rate. The trimmed-mean CPI, which excludes the 8% fastest- and 8% slowest-rising components by weight and averages the remainder, rose 4.5%. Though volatile, those suggest the current core inflation rate is more likely to go up than down in the near future.

         That core rate is 2.8% using the CPI, and 3.1% using the Fed’s preferred index. The optimists (myself included) thought inflation was underpinned by one-off shocks such as tariffs and energy and, as those pressures faded, would painlessly fall back to 2%. That may still happen.

   Here’s why that is looking less likely. First, those supply shocks are filtering into a pretty broad range of categories, not just the usual suspects like airfares, and taking their time about it. Goldman Sachs predicts the residual effects could continue through the first half of 2027.

   Second, temporary price bumps become persistent when companies have pricing power, which they do now with solid economic growth and buoyant financial markets. The missing ingredient is wages, which, despite low unemployment, are growing sluggishly. But when you include benefits, labor costs don’t look so tame. And it may only be a matter of time before wages follow prices.

   If inflation were headed to 2% on its own, the Fed would only have to tap the brakes lightly. If it is stuck around 3%, the Fed actually has to create some slack in the economy, through slower growth and higher unemployment. That will involve considerably higher interest rates.

   How much pain could that involve? The 2-year Treasury yield, a barometer of future Fed actions, is 0.25 percentage point below the 10-year yield. If it rises above the 10-year yield (an “inverted yield curve”), it is time to start thinking about recession.

Start shopping for home chefs, jetsetters, or tech enthusiasts in your life.   EXPLORE  >       What I’m Following   Financial advice in retirement: A new study finds retirees who have financial advisers keep 30 to 40 percentage points more of their portfolios in equities than nonadvised retirees, target-date funds or rules of thumb. Allison Cole of Arizona State University and three co-authors attribute this not to advisers’ incentives to market stocks, but to advisers’ own preferences: They themselves have above-average equity allocations, even after they stop advising clients. Retirees tend to underinvest in equities, given their large, stable pension incomes. Retirees’ trust in their advisers overcomes this risk aversion, which improves returns and defrays the cost of advice.

   New affordability policy ideas: Government would put ceilings on upfront costs for housing and healthcare, under proposals from the Kitchen Table Project, a policy group led by former Biden economic adviser Lael Brainard. Brainard envisions a government cap on out-of-pocket healthcare spending : copays for doctor visits, drugs, etc., paid for with savings from restricting the prices hospitals charge in highly concentrated markets. On housing, Kitchen Table proposes government-insured mortgages with a down payment of just $1,000 for first-time buyers. A small interest premium would cover credit risk. “Why not let people start building equity right away: mortgages instead of rent?” Brainard told my colleague Matt Grossman last week.

         Can a low-hire, low-fire labor market be healthy? Fed governor Christopher Waller isn’t so sure. Yes, unemployment and layoffs are low. But sluggish “churn”—job turnover as people quit in favor of better opportunities— suggests something is amiss . “I believe this churn is what leads to the exceptional performance of the U.S. economy,” Waller said Tuesday, making for better matches and higher productivity. Economic uncertainty and a big re-sorting of workers after the pandemic a few years ago could be to blame for the lull, he said. “I worry that today’s labor market dynamism may be low due to impediments to mobility that are affecting long-term and youth unemployment, and this may lead to a less-efficient distribution of workers across jobs,” he said.

   Tariffs top Mississippi senator-elect’s priorities: Democrat Scott Colom was declared the winner of Mississippi’s Senate race , becoming the state’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era. Asked Tuesday what his priority was, he said tariffs. Congress has “got to get tariff policy back. We don’t need tariff policy that is based on the ego of the president, who he’s upset with, leverage for foreign policy. Tariffs are about economic policy.”

       More From WSJ     ARMSTRONG INTERNATIONAL   • Why was a small industrial vent designed during the Nixon administration suddenly selling faster than its manufacturer could fill orders ? (You probably don’t have to click the link to guess.)

   • Bruce Krinsky tried to make furniture in America , just as President Trump wanted. He couldn’t. One night, he said, he was the last person at his North Carolina plant and thought of his great uncle working at a garment factory in New York’s Lower East Side generations ago. “For me to be a factory closing down the lights, it felt like I was going backward.”

   • “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.” United Airlines Chief Executive Scott Kirby explains why the airline won’t allow AI agents to buy tickets on behalf of fliers.

       What to Watch   Fedspeak 

   • Hawkish remarks Tuesday from two Fed voters, Lorie Logan and Christopher Waller, put a half-point rate increase on the table for December. Comments from John Williams (6:30 p.m. ET Thursday) and Philip Jefferson (7 p.m. ET Friday) could clarify how seriously the committee is taking that idea.

   Thursday 

   • 10 a.m. ET: Economists estimate October existing home sales ticked down to 3.84 million, from 3.99 million in September.

   Friday 

   • 8:30 a.m. ET: The producer-price index is expected to rise by 0.4% in October, or 0.3% excluding food and energy. Analysts will use the report to refine their estimates for the October personal-consumption expenditures inflation reading (the CPI report Tuesday suggested it is running hot).

       You Have Thoughts   In Tuesday’s newsletter , we told you about Berkeley economist Jon Steinsson’s theory that while AI may “commodify” labor and reduce wages, it “does not imply a job apocalypse.” Arkansas reader Joseph Somerville disagreed: 

   This is, de facto, a job apocalypse; simple labor economics. People trade leisure time to work because the benefit of working outweighs the sacrifice of leisure time. We already face these issues because of current prices. There are capable workers who ask the question: Why would I work, when the marginal benefit does not match the sacrifice? 

   Thoughts on what you just read? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me at wsjeconomics@wsj.com .   Include your state (or country) to be considered for publication. 

       What I’m Reading   • Nick Clegg, Meta’s former head of global affairs, writes: “Many of the tech CEOs who wanted to attach themselves to Trump seemed to think that his victory marked a permanent political shift—that the pendulum would never swing back. So they immediately doubled down.” ( The Atlantic )

   • Palantir CEO Alex Karp, who once called Democrats “totally irresponsible,” now says “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.” ( Politico )

The Inflation Fight May Be About to Turn Painful
 
Plus, retirees’ investments, the affordability agenda and the downsides of a boring job market
 

We may look back on October’s consumer-price index as an inflection point, when the balance of risks flipped toward a painful rather than painless inflation cure.

 

The consumer-price index rose 0.4%, and the core index, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3%. Anything over 0.2% is incompatible with the Federal Reserve’s 2% target, and this was the third 0.3% increase in a row.

 

Prior hot readings could be chalked up to something specific—energy, or used cars, or cellphone plans. Not this one.  

 

You can see this in two Cleveland Fed measures that remove outliers. The median CPI, which tracks the component whose expenditure weight is in the 50th percentile of price changes, rose at a 3.7% annual rate. The trimmed-mean CPI, which excludes the 8% fastest- and 8% slowest-rising components by weight and averages the remainder, rose 4.5%. Though volatile, those suggest the current core inflation rate is more likely to go up than down in the near future.

 
 
 
 

That core rate is 2.8% using the CPI, and 3.1% using the Fed’s preferred index. The optimists (myself included) thought inflation was underpinned by one-off shocks such as tariffs and energy and, as those pressures faded, would painlessly fall back to 2%. That may still happen.

 

Here’s why that is looking less likely. First, those supply shocks are filtering into a pretty broad range of categories, not just the usual suspects like airfares, and taking their time about it. Goldman Sachs predicts the residual effects could continue through the first half of 2027.

 

Second, temporary price bumps become persistent when companies have pricing power, which they do now with solid economic growth and buoyant financial markets. The missing ingredient is wages, which, despite low unemployment, are growing sluggishly. But when you include benefits, labor costs don’t look so tame. And it may only be a matter of time before wages follow prices.

 

If inflation were headed to 2% on its own, the Fed would only have to tap the brakes lightly. If it is stuck around 3%, the Fed actually has to create some slack in the economy, through slower growth and higher unemployment. That will involve considerably higher interest rates.

 

How much pain could that involve? The 2-year Treasury yield, a barometer of future Fed actions, is 0.25 percentage point below the 10-year yield. If it rises above the 10-year yield (an “inverted yield curve”), it is time to start thinking about recession.

What I’m Following

 

Financial advice in retirement: A new study finds retirees who have financial advisers keep 30 to 40 percentage points more of their portfolios in equities than nonadvised retirees, target-date funds or rules of thumb. Allison Cole of Arizona State University and three co-authors attribute this not to advisers’ incentives to market stocks, but to advisers’ own preferences: They themselves have above-average equity allocations, even after they stop advising clients. Retirees tend to underinvest in equities, given their large, stable pension incomes. Retirees’ trust in their advisers overcomes this risk aversion, which improves returns and defrays the cost of advice.

 

New affordability policy ideas: Government would put ceilings on upfront costs for housing and healthcare, under proposals from the Kitchen Table Project, a policy group led by former Biden economic adviser Lael Brainard. Brainard envisions a government cap on out-of-pocket healthcare spending: copays for doctor visits, drugs, etc., paid for with savings from restricting the prices hospitals charge in highly concentrated markets. On housing, Kitchen Table proposes government-insured mortgages with a down payment of just $1,000 for first-time buyers. A small interest premium would cover credit risk. “Why not let people start building equity right away: mortgages instead of rent?” Brainard told my colleague Matt Grossman last week.

 
 
 
 

Can a low-hire, low-fire labor market be healthy? Fed governor Christopher Waller isn’t so sure. Yes, unemployment and layoffs are low. But sluggish “churn”—job turnover as people quit in favor of better opportunities—suggests something is amiss. “I believe this churn is what leads to the exceptional performance of the U.S. economy,” Waller said Tuesday, making for better matches and higher productivity. Economic uncertainty and a big re-sorting of workers after the pandemic a few years ago could be to blame for the lull, he said. “I worry that today’s labor market dynamism may be low due to impediments to mobility that are affecting long-term and youth unemployment, and this may lead to a less-efficient distribution of workers across jobs,” he said.

 

Tariffs top Mississippi senator-elect’s priorities: Democrat Scott Colom was declared the winner of Mississippi’s Senate race, becoming the state’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era. Asked Tuesday what his priority was, he said tariffs. Congress has “got to get tariff policy back. We don’t need tariff policy that is based on the ego of the president, who he’s upset with, leverage for foreign policy. Tariffs are about economic policy.”

 
 
 

More From WSJ

 
 
ARMSTRONG INTERNATIONAL
 

• Why was a small industrial vent designed during the Nixon administration suddenly selling faster than its manufacturer could fill orders? (You probably don’t have to click the link to guess.)

 

• Bruce Krinsky tried to make furniture in America, just as President Trump wanted. He couldn’t. One night, he said, he was the last person at his North Carolina plant and thought of his great uncle working at a garment factory in New York’s Lower East Side generations ago. “For me to be a factory closing down the lights, it felt like I was going backward.”

 

• “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.” United Airlines Chief Executive Scott Kirby explains why the airline won’t allow AI agents to buy tickets on behalf of fliers.

 
 
 

What to Watch

 

Fedspeak

 

• Hawkish remarks Tuesday from two Fed voters, Lorie Logan and Christopher Waller, put a half-point rate increase on the table for December. Comments from John Williams (6:30 p.m. ET Thursday) and Philip Jefferson (7 p.m. ET Friday) could clarify how seriously the committee is taking that idea.

 

Thursday

 

• 10 a.m. ET: Economists estimate October existing home sales ticked down to 3.84 million, from 3.99 million in September.

 

Friday

 

• 8:30 a.m. ET: The producer-price index is expected to rise by 0.4% in October, or 0.3% excluding food and energy. Analysts will use the report to refine their estimates for the October personal-consumption expenditures inflation reading (the CPI report Tuesday suggested it is running hot).

 
 
 

You Have Thoughts

 

In Tuesday’s newsletter, we told you about Berkeley economist Jon Steinsson’s theory that while AI may “commodify” labor and reduce wages, it “does not imply a job apocalypse.” Arkansas reader Joseph Somerville disagreed:

 

This is, de facto, a job apocalypse; simple labor economics. People trade leisure time to work because the benefit of working outweighs the sacrifice of leisure time. We already face these issues because of current prices. There are capable workers who ask the question: Why would I work, when the marginal benefit does not match the sacrifice? 

 

Thoughts on what you just read? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me at wsjeconomics@wsj.com. Include your state (or country) to be considered for publication.

 
 
 

What I’m Reading

 

• Nick Clegg, Meta’s former head of global affairs, writes: “Many of the tech CEOs who wanted to attach themselves to Trump seemed to think that his victory marked a permanent political shift—that the pendulum would never swing back. So they immediately doubled down.” (The Atlantic)

 

• Palantir CEO Alex Karp, who once called Democrats “totally irresponsible,” now says “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.” (Politico)
